claim: Codon optimization underlies genome adaptation in broad host range parasites.
source: Here, we show that codon optimization underlies genome adaptation in broad host range parasites.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple analyses throughout the manuscript including genome-scale correlations, phylogenetic analyses, and population genetics.

claim: Longer proteins encoded by broad host range fungi likely increase natural selection on codon optimization in these species.
source: We found that the longer proteins encoded by broad host range fungi likely increase natural selection on codon optimization in these species.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling showing that longer proteins in generalists require higher codon decoding rates to achieve similar growth rates as specialists.

claim: Codon optimization correlates with host range across the fungal kingdom.
source: Accordingly, codon optimization correlates with host range across the fungal kingdom.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical correlation analysis of 36 fungal species showing Spearman rho = 0.82, p=7.1 10−10.

claim: Biased patterns of synonymous substitutions underpin increased codon optimization in a generalist but not a specialist fungal pathogen.
source: At the species level, biased patterns of synonymous substitutions underpin increased codon optimization in a generalist but not a specialist fungal pathogen.
evidence: Supported by SNP analysis in S. sclerotiorum and Z. tritici populations showing differential patterns of synonymous substitutions.

claim: Virulence genes were consistently enriched in highly codon-optimized genes of generalist but not specialist species.
source: Virulence genes were consistently enriched in highly codon-optimized genes of generalist but not specialist species.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of host-induced genes and secretome genes across multiple fungal species.

claim: Codon optimization is related to the capacity of parasites to colonize multiple hosts.
source: We conclude that codon optimization is related to the capacity of parasites to colonize multiple hosts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including genome-scale correlations, phylogenetic patterns, and functional gene enrichment.

claim: Secreted proteins were ~14.8% longer in generalists than in specialists (365 and 318 codons respectively).
source: In average, secreted proteins were ~14.8% longer in generalists than in specialists (365 and 318 codons respectively; Welch's t-test p<10−08).
evidence: Statistical comparison of protein lengths across 13 specialist and 15 generalist fungal species.

claim: Intracellular proteins were ~10.1% longer in average in generalists than in specialists (381 and 346 codons respectively).
source: Intracellular proteins were also longer in average in generalists than in specialists (~10.1% longer with 381 and 346 codons respectively; Welch's t-test p<10−08)
evidence: Statistical comparison of protein lengths across 13 specialist and 15 generalist fungal species.

claim: Ribosomal proteins were slightly shorter in average in generalists than in specialists (~1.2% shorter with 189 and 192 codons respectively).
source: whereas ribosomal proteins were slightly shorter in average in generalists than in specialists (~1.2% shorter with 189 and 192 codons respectively; Welch's t-test p<10−04).
evidence: Statistical comparison of protein lengths across 13 specialist and 15 generalist fungal species.

claim: In yeast, codon decoding rate varies from 10 to 28 codons per second, with an average of 20 codons per second.
source: In yeast, codon decoding rate varies from 10 to 28 codons per second, with an average of 20 codons per second (Gardin et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gardin et al., 2014).

claim: Cells of specialists achieved higher maximal growth rates than cells of generalists at a given codon decoding rate.
source: Cells of specialists achieved higher maximal growth rates than cells of generalists at a given codon decoding rate.
evidence: Demonstrated by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: To achieve a growth rate of 4000 cells per 24 hr, the codon decoding rate should be 21.7 codons per second in generalists but only 19.9 codons per second in specialists.
source: For instance, in order to achieve a growth rate of 4000 cells per 24 hr, the codon decoding rate should be 21.7 codons per second in generalists but only 19.9 codons per second in specialists.
evidence: Calculated from the computational model of cell translation machinery.

claim: Secreted proteins of the generalist Botrytis cinerea were in average ~73% longer (394 amino acids) than secreted proteins of the specialist Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (228 amino acids).
source: For instance, secreted proteins of the generalist Botrytis cinerea were in average ~73% longer (394 amino acids) than secreted proteins of the specialist Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (228 amino acids; Welch's t-test p<10−08).
evidence: Statistical comparison of protein lengths between specific generalist and specialist species.

claim: S values ranged from −0.032 (Puccinia graminis) to 0.843 (Cryptococcus neoformans), with an average of 0.374.
source: S values ranged from −0.032 (Puccinia graminis) to 0.843 (Cryptococcus neoformans), with an average of 0.374.
evidence: Calculated S values for codon optimization across 36 fungal species.

claim: Codon optimization at the whole genome scale increased with host range (Spearman rho = 0.82, p=7.1 10−10).
source: We performed a correlation analysis and found that codon optimization at the whole genome scale increased with host range (Spearman rho = 0.82, p=7.1 10−10, Figure 2A).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis across 36 fungal species, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Generalist species had an average S of 0.58, whereas the average S was 0.23 for specialists.
source: Generalist species had an average S of 0.58, whereas the average S was 0.23 for specialists.
evidence: Calculated from S values across generalist and specialist species.

claim: The significance of the correlation between host range and genome scale codon optimization using Felsenstein's phylogenetic independent contrasts yielded Spearman rho of 0.6 (p=1.5 10−05).
source: We verified the significance of the correlation between host range and genome scale codon optimization using Felsenstein's phylogenetic independent contrasts, and obtained Spearman rho of 0.6 (p=1.5 10−05).
evidence: Phylogenetic independent contrasts analysis to control for phylogenetic relationships.

claim: SCAI increased with host range (Spearman rho = 0.61, p=9.0 10−06 under phylogenetic independent contrasts).
source: SCAI increased with host range (Spearman rho = 0.61, p=9.0 10−06 under phylogenetic independent contrasts)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis using codon adaptation index.

claim: Generalist species had an average SCAI of 0.61, whereas the average SCAI was 0.26 for specialists.
source: and generalist species had an average SCAI of 0.61, whereas the average SCAI was 0.26 for specialists.
evidence: Calculated from SCAI values across generalist and specialist species.

claim: SscnRCA increased with host range (Spearman rho = 0.59, p=2.7 10−05 under phylogenetic independent contrasts).
source: SscnRCA increased with host range (Spearman rho = 0.59, p=2.7 10−05 under phylogenetic independent contrasts)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis using self-consistent normalized Relative Codon Adaptation index.

claim: Generalist species had an average SscnRCA of 0.67, whereas the average SscnRCA was 0.32 for specialists.
source: and generalist species had an average SscnRCA of 0.67, whereas the average SscnRCA was 0.32 for specialists.
evidence: Calculated from SscnRCA values across generalist and specialist species.

claim: The tRNA adaptation indices (tAIs) were significantly higher in the orthologs of generalist genomes (median value is 0.361) than in orthologs of specialist genomes (median value is 0.337).
source: The tRNA adaptation indices (tAIs) were significantly higher in the orthologs of generalist genomes (median value is 0.361) than in orthologs of specialist genomes (median value is 0.337; Welch's t-test p<0.01) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of tAIs in 1620 core ortholog genes, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: S is significantly higher for COGs in generalist genomes (median is 0.774) than in specialist genomes (median is 0.167).
source: We calculated S for COGs in each genome and found that S is significantly higher for COGs in generalist genomes (median is 0.774) than in specialist genomes (median is 0.167; Welch's t-test p=9.9 10−06) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of S values for core ortholog genes, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Codon optimization was generally lower in non-parasitic fungi than in their generalist relatives (average values for non parasitic fungi were S = 0.157, SCAI = 0.315 and SscnRCA = 0.354).
source: We determined the degree of codon optimization in non-parasitic fungal genomes and found that codon optimization was generally lower in non-parasitic fungi than in their generalist relatives (average values for non parasitic fungi were S = 0.157, SCAI = 0.315 and SscnRCA = 0.354).
evidence: Calculated codon optimization values for 9 non-parasitic fungal species.

claim: The fungal parasites species used in this work represented four independent evolutionary paths to extreme generalism (over 100 host genera) with non-parasitic or specialists in the same clade, in the Chytridiomycota, the Agaricomycotina, the Leotiomycetes and the Sordariomycetes.
source: The fungal parasites species used in this work represented four independent evolutionary paths to extreme generalism (over 100 host genera) with non-parasitic or specialists in the same clade, in the Chytridiomycota, the Agaricomycotina, the Leotiomycetes and the Sordariomycetes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A identifying independent evolutionary origins of generalism.

claim: In all four clades, generalism was associated with an increase in genomic codon adaptation compared to related non-parasitic or specialist species and to the reconstructed ancestral state.
source: In all four clades, generalism was associated with an increase in genomic codon adaptation compared to related non-parasitic or specialist species and to the reconstructed ancestral state.
evidence: Phylogenetic reconstruction of ancestral states and comparison with extant species.

claim: In the Leotiomycetes, the generalist parasites Botrytis cinerea and Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (>300 host genera) both had S > 0.5, whereas the non-parasitic Oidiodendron maius and the host specialists Erysiphe necator and Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici had S < 0.2.
source: For instance, in the Leotiomycetes, the generalist parasites Botrytis cinerea and Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (>300 host genera) both had S > 0.5, whereas the non-parasitic Oidiodendron maius and the host specialists Erysiphe necator and Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici had S < 0.2.
evidence: Specific example from phylogenetic analysis showing codon optimization differences within a clade.

claim: The reconstructed ancestral state for the Leotiomycetes clade was S = 0.37.
source: The reconstructed ancestral state for this clade was S = 0.37.
evidence: Ancestral state reconstruction using ML estimation.

claim: The correlation coefficient between genome-scale codon optimization and host range were between 0.64 and 0.84 for S, SCAI and SscnRCA at the Phylum level in Basidiomycetes and Ascomycetes, and across phyla in non-Dikarya fungi.
source: The correlation coefficient between genome-scale codon optimization and host range were between 0.64 and 0.84 for S, SCAI and SscnRCA at the Phylum level in Basidiomycetes and Ascomycetes, and across phyla in non-Dikarya fungi.
evidence: Sub-Kingdom level correlation analyses to test robustness across phylogeny.

claim: Blomberg's K = 0.28 and Pagel's λ = 0.62 for phylogenetic signal in genome scale codon optimization along the fungal tree.
source: We obtained Blomberg's K = 0.28 and Pagel's λ = 0.62.
evidence: Quantitative measures of phylogenetic signal calculated from the data.

claim: Both measures indicated that evolution of codon optimization is not correlated with the phylogeny along the tree at p<0.01.
source: Both measures indicated that evolution of codon optimization is not correlated with the phylogeny along the tree at p<0.01.
evidence: Statistical interpretation of Blomberg's K and Pagel's λ values.

claim: Correlations between phylogenetic distance and codon optimization were insignificant (in the range −0.05 to 0.1) along the whole tree.
source: Correlations were insignificant (in the range −0.05 to 0.1) along the whole tree.
evidence: Correlogram analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: S. sclerotiorum is the causal agent of Sclerotinia rot disease, is notorious for its broad host range encompassing several hundreds of plant genera, and shows strong signatures of codon optimization (S = 0.52).
source: S. sclerotiorum is the causal agent of Sclerotinia rot disease, is notorious for its broad host range encompassing several hundreds of plant genera, and shows strong signatures of codon optimization (S = 0.52).
evidence: Background information on S. sclerotiorum and its calculated S value.

claim: tRNA concentrations determined by small RNA sequencing strongly correlated with the number of tRNA genomic copies, tRNA adaptive values and codon usage in S. sclerotiorum.
source: As expected under strong codon optimization, tRNA concentrations determined by small RNA sequencing strongly correlated with the number of tRNA genomic copies, tRNA adaptive values (calculated according to [dos Reis et al., 2004]) and codon usage in S. sclerotiorum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Small RNA sequencing data showing correlations, presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Z. tritici is a host-specific plant pathogenic fungus with weak codon optimization (S = −0.02).
source: We used 131,138 genome-wide coding SNPs of nine isolates of the host-specific plant pathogenic fungus Zymoseptoria tritici (Croll et al., 2013) as a reference species with weak codon optimization (S = −0.02).
evidence: Background information on Z. tritici and its calculated S value, with citation to SNP data source.

claim: The SNP frequency was higher in the Z. tritici population (1.196 SNP.Kb−1.isolate−1) compared to S. sclerotiorum (0.416 SNP.kb−1.isolate−1).
source: Overall, the SNP frequency was higher in the Z. tritici population (1.196 SNP.Kb−1.isolate−1) compared to S. sclerotiorum (0.416 SNP.kb−1.isolate−1).
evidence: Calculated from genome-wide SNP data in both species.

claim: Frequency of codon variants negatively correlated with the number of tRNA genomic copies in S. sclerotiorum (Pearson = −0.60, p = 4.6 10−07) but not in Z. tritici (Pearson = 0.06, p = 0.62).
source: Frequency of codon variants negatively correlated with the number of tRNA genomic copies in S. sclerotiorum (Pearson = −0.60, p = 4.6 10−07) but not in Z. tritici (Pearson = 0.06, p = 0.62) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of SNP patterns with tRNA gene copies, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the Z. tritici population, SNP frequencies were not significantly different between optimal and non-optimal codons.
source: In the Z. tritici population, SNP frequencies were not significantly different between optimal and non-optimal codons.
evidence: Analysis of SNP patterns in optimal vs non-optimal codons.

claim: Synonymous SNP frequencies were on average ~1.7-fold lower in optimal codons than in non-optimal codons in S. sclerotiorum (Welch's t-test p=1.3 10−03).
source: By contrast, synonymous SNP frequencies were on average ~1.7-fold lower in optimal codons than in non-optimal codons in S. sclerotiorum (Welch's t-test p=1.3 10−03) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of SNP frequencies in optimal vs non-optimal codons, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: S. sclerotiorum genome is AT-rich (41.8% GC).
source: Although S. sclerotiorum genome is AT-rich (41.8% GC), synonymous SNPs showed no bias toward AT conversion
evidence: Calculated GC content of the S. sclerotiorum genome.

claim: Synonymous SNPs in S. sclerotiorum showed no bias toward AT conversion.
source: Although S. sclerotiorum genome is AT-rich (41.8% GC), synonymous SNPs showed no bias toward AT conversion, suggesting that synonymous SNPs deviated from neutral patterns (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Analysis of SNP patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adjusted variant frequencies in S. sclerotiorum were similar in intergenic nucleotide triplets and in non-optimal codons but significantly lower in optimal codons (~1.53-fold lower, Welch's t-test p= 1.0 10−11).
source: Furthermore, adjusted variant frequencies in S. sclerotiorum were similar in intergenic nucleotide triplets and in non-optimal codons but significantly lower in optimal codons (~1.53-fold lower, Welch's t-test p= 1.0 10−11) (Figure 4B)
evidence: Statistical comparison of variant frequencies across different genomic contexts, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The codon SNP patterns determined experimentally converge toward increased codon optimality in S. sclerotiorum genome, whereas SNP patterns observed in Z. tritici genome and random mutation patterns do not.
source: This demonstrated that the codon SNP patterns determined experimentally converge toward increased codon optimality in S. sclerotiorum genome, whereas SNP patterns observed in Z. tritici genome and random mutation patterns do not.
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 4C demonstrating evolutionary trajectories.

claim: Patterns of evolution toward increased codon optimality were detected in S. sclerotiorum but not in Z. tritici populations, and deviate significantly from neutral evolution.
source: Thus, patterns of evolution toward increased codon optimality were detected in S. sclerotiorum but not in Z. tritici populations, and deviate significantly from neutral evolution.
evidence: Conclusion from simulation analysis comparing observed vs random mutation patterns.

claim: A total of 14 species showed signatures of selection for codon optimization with a p<0.1, among which one was a specialist (M. roreri) and one had eight host genera (P. destructans).
source: A total of 14 species showed signatures of selection for codon optimization with a p<0.1, among which one was a specialist (M. roreri) and one had eight host genera (P. destructans).
evidence: Permutation test results across fungal genomes.

claim: Twelve out of 15 (80%) generalist species showed selection for codon optimization with a p<0.1.
source: Twelve out of 15 (80%) generalist species showed selection for codon optimization with a p<0.1, confirming that adaptive translation is stronger in generalist species.
evidence: Permutation test results for generalist species.

claim: Natural selection on protein translation efficiency or accuracy drives evolution toward codon optimization in generalist parasites through biased synonymous SNPs.
source: We conclude that natural selection on protein translation efficiency or accuracy drives evolution toward codon optimization in generalist parasites through biased synonymous SNPs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SNP analysis and simulation results.

claim: Host-induced genes were enriched ~3.1-fold among the top 10% codon-adapted genes in generalist parasites but not in specialists.
source: We found that host-induced genes were enriched ~3.1-fold among the top 10% codon-adapted genes in generalist parasites but not in specialists.
evidence: Analysis of host-induced genes across 15 fungal species.

claim: Genes induced during host colonization distributed predominantly among genes with high codon adaptation indices in generalist but not in specialist parasites.
source: Overall, genes induced during host colonization distributed predominantly among genes with high codon adaptation indices in generalist but not in specialist parasites (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Distribution analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Secretome genes were enriched over 1.6-fold among the top 10% codon-adapted genes in generalist parasites but only ~1.2-fold in specialists and non-parasitic fungi.
source: We found that secretome genes were enriched over 1.6-fold among the top 10% codon-adapted genes in generalist parasites but only ~1.2-fold in specialists and non-parasitic fungi.
evidence: Analysis of secretome genes across 45 fungal species.

claim: Predicted secretome genes distributed predominantly among genes with high codon adaptation indices in generalist parasites but not in specialist and non parasitic fungi.
source: Overall, predicted secretome genes distributed predominantly among genes with high codon adaptation indices in generalist parasites but not in specialist and non parasitic fungi (Figure 5B).
evidence: Distribution analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In non-parasitic fungi, S was similar for secreted and non-secreted proteins.
source: In our genome set, non-parasitic fungi had similar S for secreted and non-secreted proteins.
evidence: Comparison of S values for different protein categories in non-parasitic fungi.

claim: The average S for secreted proteins (0.212) was slightly higher than for non-secreted proteins (0.137) in specialists (Student's paired t-test p=0.054).
source: The average S for secreted proteins (0.212) was slightly higher than for non-secreted proteins (0.137) in specialists (Student's paired t-test p=0.054).
evidence: Statistical comparison of S values for secreted vs non-secreted proteins in specialists.

claim: In generalists, the average S for secreted proteins (0.661) was significantly higher than for non secreted proteins (0.558, Student's paired t-test p=1.12 10−03).
source: In generalists, the average S for secreted proteins (0.661) was significantly higher than for non secreted proteins (0.558, Student's paired t-test p=1.12 10−03).
evidence: Statistical comparison of S values for secreted vs non-secreted proteins in generalists.

claim: GOs related to translation and central metabolism showed higher codon optimization in generalists than in specialists.
source: Together with secreted enzymes, GOs related to translation and central metabolism showed higher codon optimization in generalists than in specialists.
evidence: Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: GOs related to transcription, transposable elements and phosphorelay signal transduction were better optimized in specialists than in generalists.
source: Conversely, GOs related to transcription, transposable elements and phosphorelay signal transduction were better optimized in specialists than in generalists.
evidence: Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: High codon optimization is an adaptation to host colonization and particularly to the colonization of multiple hosts.
source: These results suggest that high codon optimization is an adaptation to host colonization and particularly to the colonization of multiple hosts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple analyses of host-induced genes, secretome genes, and functional enrichment.

claim: The host range of a parasite has a central influence on the emergence and spread of disease.
source: The host range of a parasite has a central influence on the emergence and spread of disease (Woolhouse and Gowtage-Sequeria, 2005).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Woolhouse and Gowtage-Sequeria, 2005).

claim: There is a clear demarcation between specialist parasites that can only infect one or a few closely related host species and generalists that can infect more than a hundred unrelated host species.
source: There is a clear demarcation between specialist parasites that can only infect one or a few closely related host species and generalists that can infect more than a hundred unrelated host species (Woolhouse et al., 2001; Barrett et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Woolhouse et al., 2001; Barrett et al., 2009).

claim: The host range is a trait constrained by ecological and physiological factors and determined by the evolutionary history of a parasite and its potential hosts.
source: The host range is a trait constrained by ecological and physiological factors and determined by the evolutionary history of a parasite and its potential hosts (Poulin and Keeney, 2008).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Poulin and Keeney, 2008).

claim: Host specialization is a frequent pattern in living systems that was proposed to result from tradeoffs in performance on multiple hosts.
source: Host specialization is a frequent pattern in living systems that was proposed to result from tradeoffs in performance on multiple hosts (Joshi and Thompson, 1995).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Joshi and Thompson, 1995).

claim: Optimization by natural selection of parasite proteins functioning in the interaction with a given host may be detrimental to their function in another species.
source: At the molecular level, optimization by natural selection of parasite proteins functioning in the interaction with a given host may be detrimental to their function in another species (Dodds and Rathjen, 2010; Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Dodds and Rathjen, 2010; Dong et al., 2014).

claim: Genomic analyses of obligate specialist parasites revealed massive losses of enzymes unnecessary for growth and reproduction on living hosts.
source: Genomic analyses of obligate specialist parasites revealed massive losses of enzymes unnecessary for growth and reproduction on living hosts (Schirawski et al., 2010; Spanu et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Schirawski et al., 2010; Spanu et al., 2010).

claim: The genome of the powdery mildew pathogen Blumeria graminis f. sp. hordei harbors 180 SSPs of about 100–150 amino acids.
source: For instance, the genome of the powdery mildew pathogen Blumeria graminis f. sp. hordei harbors 180 SSPs of about 100–150 amino acids (Pedersen et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Pedersen et al., 2012).

claim: SSPs of specialist fungi often show evidence of diversifying-selection leading to extensive changes in their protein sequence.
source: SSPs of specialist fungi often show evidence of diversifying-selection leading to extensive changes in their protein sequence (Stukenbrock et al., 2011; Pedersen et al., 2012; Hacquard et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Stukenbrock et al., 2011; Pedersen et al., 2012; Hacquard et al., 2013).

claim: The secretion of a battery of degrading enzymes is crucial for the parasitic success of generalists.
source: By contrast, the secretion of a battery of degrading enzymes is crucial for the parasitic success of generalists (Hu et al., 2014; Kubicek et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Hu et al., 2014; Kubicek et al., 2014).

claim: The genomes of generalist fungi contain in average ~3 times more carbohydrate activity enzymes (CAZYmes) than specialist fungi.
source: The genomes of generalist fungi notably contain in average ~3 times more carbohydrate activity enzymes (CAZYmes) than specialist fungi (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Zhao et al., 2013).

claim: Rhizoctonia solani AG2-2IIIB contains over 1000 CAZYme genes.
source: For instance, Rhizoctonia solani AG2-2IIIB contains over 1000 CAZYme genes (Wibberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Wibberg et al., 2016).

claim: Protein translation is the largest consumer of energy during cellular proliferation.
source: Protein translation is the largest consumer of energy during cellular proliferation
evidence: General knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: Secreted proteins are not recycled like other cellular proteins.
source: and because secreted proteins are not recycled like other cellular proteins, strong constraints exist to reduce the synthetic cost of secreted proteins in microbes (Smith and Chapman, 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Smith and Chapman, 2010).

claim: The differential use of synonymous codons in a genome, or codon usage bias, affects gene expression level, protein folding, translation efficiency and accuracy.
source: The differential use of synonymous codons in a genome, or codon usage bias, affects gene expression level, protein folding, translation efficiency and accuracy (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).

claim: The co-evolution of codons with the genomic tRNA complement, leading to codon optimization, results from the combination of neutral processes and selection for the optimization of protein translation.
source: In particular, the co-evolution of codons with the genomic tRNA complement, leading to codon optimization, results from the combination of neutral processes and selection for the optimization of protein translation (Hershberg and Petrov, 2008; Shah and Gilchrist, 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Hershberg and Petrov, 2008; Shah and Gilchrist, 2011).

claim: Natural selection for the optimization of protein translation, through ribosome pausing time, translation error rates and co-translational protein folding, has been widely associated with codon usage biases.
source: Natural selection for the optimization of protein translation, through ribosome pausing time, translation error rates and co-translational protein folding, has been widely associated with codon usage biases (Drummond and Wilke, 2008; Tuller et al., 2010; Shah and Gilchrist, 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Drummond and Wilke, 2008; Tuller et al., 2010; Shah and Gilchrist, 2011).

claim: The probability of protein translation error increases with protein length.
source: Because the probability of protein translation error increases with protein length, selection for translation accuracy can be higher in genes encoding long proteins, as was observed in E. coli (Eyre-Walker, 1996).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Eyre-Walker, 1996).

claim: Selection for translation accuracy can be higher in genes encoding long proteins, as was observed in E. coli.
source: Because the probability of protein translation error increases with protein length, selection for translation accuracy can be higher in genes encoding long proteins, as was observed in E. coli (Eyre-Walker, 1996).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Eyre-Walker, 1996).

claim: Codon usage bias increases with the evolutionary age of genes, the frequency of codons optimal for translation being significantly higher at codons for conserved amino acids.
source: Codon usage bias also increases with the evolutionary age of genes, the frequency of codons optimal for translation being significantly higher at codons for conserved amino acids (Marais and Duret, 2001; Prat et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Marais and Duret, 2001; Prat et al., 2009).

claim: The cost of protein translation leads to a tradeoff between protein production and cell growth rate.
source: The cost of protein translation leads to a tradeoff between protein production and cell growth rate (Scott et al., 2010; Shah et al., 2013; Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Scott et al., 2010; Shah et al., 2013; Kafri et al., 2016).

claim: Codon optimization impacts cell growth in selective environments.
source: Codon optimization therefore impacts cell growth in selective environments (Botzman and Margalit, 2011; Krisko et al., 2014)
evidence: Cited from published literature (Botzman and Margalit, 2011; Krisko et al., 2014).

claim: Codon optimization could positively impact on the performances of parasites regardless of the host they encounter.
source: and could positively impact on the performances of parasites regardless of the host they encounter.
evidence: Logical inference from the relationship between codon optimization and cell growth.

claim: Generalist lineages performing better on average on their set of available hosts than co-occurring specialist competitors is predicted by the 'jack of all trades, master of none' theoretical model.
source: This hypothesis would be consistent with generalist lineages performing better on average on their set of available hosts than co-occurring specialist competitors to persist in the biota, as predicted by the 'jack of all trades, master of none' theoretical model (Futuyma and Moreno, 1988).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Futuyma and Moreno, 1988).

claim: High codon optimization and broad host ranges co-evolved multiple times independently through fungal phylogeny.
source: High codon optimization and broad host ranges co-evolved multiple times independently through fungal phylogeny.
evidence: Conclusion from phylogenetic analysis showing independent evolutionary origins.

claim: Signatures of purifying natural selection acting on optimal codons were detected in the generalist parasite only.
source: We detected signatures of purifying natural selection acting on optimal codons in the generalist parasite only.
evidence: Conclusion from SNP pattern analysis comparing S. sclerotiorum and Z. tritici.

claim: The efficiency and accuracy of protein translation constrains cell growth rate and depends on sequence properties of expressed proteins.
source: The efficiency and accuracy of protein translation constrains cell growth rate and depends on sequence properties of expressed proteins (Ingolia et al., 2009; Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Ingolia et al., 2009; Kafri et al., 2016).

claim: The likelihood that a parasite can infect two host species decreases continuously with phylogenetic distance between the hosts.
source: The likelihood that a parasite can infect two host species decreases continuously with phylogenetic distance between the hosts (Gilbert and Webb, 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gilbert and Webb, 2007).

claim: Gilbert and Webb reported that the proportion of hosts colonized was about ~20% at a 300 Mya phylogenetic distance, decreasing logarithmically.
source: In their study, Gilbert and Webb reported that the proportion of hosts colonized was about ~20% at a 300 Mya phylogenetic distance, decreasing logarithmically.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Gilbert and Webb, 2007).

claim: The adaptive evolution of effectors that increase the colonization of one host species also increases the risk of detection in other host species by triggering their immune system.
source: The adaptive evolution of effectors that increase the colonization of one host species also increases the risk of detection in other host species by triggering their immune system.
